tldr: NeoWorld-Pro is a framework that constructs interactive 3D scenes from a single RGB image without interpenetration or collapse, ready for robot manipulation by combining multimodal LLM code generation with a physics simulation validation loop.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of NeoWorld-Pro. It estimates the scene hierarchy from a single image, procedurally generates each object via Blender scripts, and establishes a valid, crash-free scene through a dual physics-in-the-loop mechanism: an object-level articulation/physics refinement loop and a scene-level placement optimization loop using CEM.
overview:
Training Embodied AI agents to operate in the real world requires high-quality simulation environments that are not just visually accurate, but physically interactive. However, existing methods for reconstructing 3D scenes from a single photo tend to focus primarily on matching visual shapes such as meshes or point clouds. Consequently, movable joints like drawers often fail to articulate, and objects can intersect and explode or collapse upon simulator startup, posing severe obstacles for direct use in robot experiments.

To address this, the authors propose "NeoWorld-Pro", reformulating single-image scene reconstruction as an automated executable program generation task. Leveraging the commonsense reasoning and code synthesis abilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), it writes object geometry and articulated structures (URDF) as Blender Python scripts. Most importantly, it introduces a "physics-in-the-loop" mechanism: generated code is executed in physics engines like Isaac Sim to check whether objects fall during free drop or whether joints move as intended under external forces. If a test fails, the code is iteratively rewritten.

Experiments on a newly collected benchmark of 90 articulated object categories and 30 scene assemblies show dramatic improvements in articulation accuracy and geometry quality over conventional open-loop reconstruction methods. Furthermore, NeoWorld-Pro completely eliminates object interpenetration and stably runs fine-grained downstream tasks in simulation, such as robotic test-tube grasping/insertion and domino toppling.
contributions: Formulated interactive scene construction from a single-view image as an MLLM-based procedural code generation task, significantly reducing reliance on specific asset databases and pre-trained categories.

Proposed an object-level physics-in-the-loop mechanism that feeds dynamic simulation behaviors (e.g., collisions, collapses) back into the MLLM to autonomously refine articulated structures and inertial parameters.
Constructed a scene-level optimization framework integrating the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM), physics simulation, and MLLM evaluations to optimize overall scene placement and scale.
Established a new simulation evaluation benchmark comprising 90 articulated object categories and 30 USD-format scenes with robot manipulation tasks, validating the framework's effectiveness.

sections.heading: Building "Simulation-Ready Environments" Directly from a Photo
sections.summary: This paper presents a new approach to automate Real-to-Sim transfer for robot learning. To create environments with proper articulation and no physical interpenetration rather than purely visual 3D reconstructions, it integrates program synthesis with physics simulator verification loops.
sections.details:
Setting up Real-to-Sim environments for robots to learn physical manipulation requires enormous manual effort and does not scale easily. Therefore, techniques that automatically generate simulation-ready assets from a single photograph are in high demand.

However, conventional approaches reconstructing URDFs (the standard format defining kinematic joints and links for robots and objects) from single images face three main hurdles:
- They primarily target isolated, single objects, neglecting interactions and spatial relationships in multi-object scenes.
- They depend heavily on retrieving CAD models from pre-built 3D libraries or on limited category knowledge, struggling with unseen shapes.
- They are open-loop processes without corrective feedback, meaning object interpenetrations and physical implausibilities cannot be detected or resolved.

To solve these problems, the authors developed "NeoWorld-Pro" (where Pro stands for Programming). Instead of treating a scene merely as dense point clouds or meshes, it shifts the paradigm to an executable and editable procedural program. Utilizing the spatial reasoning and commonsense priors of MLLMs, it synthesizes Python code, logically hallucinating occluded geometry such as the interior volume of closed drawers.

In addition, it embeds a "physics-in-the-loop" mechanism that runs drop tests and external force perturbation tests in physics engines like Isaac Sim. Using collision and collapse logs, it iteratively refines the code. This achieves truly simulation-ready environments that look plausible and remain stable when touched by robots.

captions.F1: Demonstration of NeoWorld-Pro and the impact of physics-in-the-loop verification. It hierarchically optimizes whether joints actuate properly under external forces (a-b), whether phone stands and dominoes remain stable under free drop (c-d), and whether downstream tasks like test-tube pick-and-place succeed (e-f).

sections.heading: From Static Geometry Matching to Code Generation with Physical Feedback
sections.summary: This section reviews prior works on articulated asset reconstruction from images/point clouds and LLM-driven 3D generation. While most existing studies rely on asset retrieval or open-loop predictions, this framework is unique in coupling zero-shot code synthesis with dynamic simulation feedback loops.
sections.details:
The related work is categorized into two main research streams to highlight the novelty of NeoWorld-Pro.

### Articulated Asset Reconstruction from Visual and Geometric Inputs
To manipulate an environment, robots require articulated models containing links and joints. Historically, approaches relied on LiDAR point clouds, multi-view captures, or paired images before and after articulation. However, acquiring such data in real-world settings is exceptionally costly.

While single-image approaches have emerged, most search for similar parts in fixed 3D mesh repositories or are constrained by training category distributions. More crucially, even when simulations are conducted, they are merely post-hoc evaluations without mechanisms to feed failure signals back into the generation pipeline for correction.

### LLMs and MLLMs as Priors for 3D Generation
Recently, studies have used LLM priors to predict part connectivity graphs (SINGAPO), draft coarse URDF templates (SPARK), or critique joint positions in an Actor-Critic format (Articulate-Anything).

Pushing this further, some methods generate URDFs and physical attributes directly via MLLMs (e.g., PhysX-Anything). However, these are frequently fine-tuned on specific articulated datasets, inheriting strong dataset biases. NeoWorld-Pro stands apart by combining zero-shot MLLM programming with dynamic simulation execution feedback, flexibly generalizing to unseen categories and intricate multi-object scene layouts without being tied to specific datasets.

sections.heading: An Architecture That Refines Code Through Two-Stage Physics Loops
sections.summary: NeoWorld-Pro is a procedural framework that generates Blender scripts from a single image and converts them into URDF and USD scenes. It achieves physically stable environments using a two-level physics validation mechanism: an object-level code refinement loop and a scene-level placement optimization loop using CEM.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Overview: Scene Reconstruction as Program Synthesis
The input is a single RGB image $I$, and the output is an interactive scene in USD (Universal Scene Description) format integrating URDF models for all objects. The pipeline uses Blender Python scripts as an intermediate representation. Treating assets as code enables direct simulation execution, seamless MLLM self-debugging, and easy re-editing.

The pipeline consists of two hierarchical physics-in-the-loop stages:
- Object-level loop: Refines discrete structures and physical properties, such as articulation limits and inertia parameters, via MLLM code editing.
- Scene-level loop: Adjusts continuous layout variables like relative positions, scales, and yaw rotations using physics-engine-guided optimization.

### 3.2 Object-Level Procedural Generation and Articulation Refinement
This stage consists of three steps:
- Step 1 (Scene Parsing): A reasoning MLLM (Qwen3.6-Plus) predicts the scene hierarchy tree (parent-child support relations, e.g., a cup on a table), 2D/3D bounding boxes, and occlusion attributes. A Critic MLLM audits bounding boxes and crops individual object regions.
- Step 2 (Procedural Asset Generation): A Programmer MLLM (GPT-5.5) sequentially drafts Python scripts for geometry generation, joint definition, and URDF export. It self-debugs runtime execution errors and writes URDFs through a critic loop comparing rendered views against input crops. This procedural synthesis automatically extrapolates occluded internal structures (such as drawer boxes behind handles) via commonsense reasoning.
- Step 3 (Object-Level Physics Validation): Exported URDFs are imported into Isaac Sim for free-drop and external force perturbation tests. Drop tests expose unbalanced mass distributions and collision mesh defects, while perturbation tests verify joint kinematics. A Critic MLLM inspects simulation keyframe videos and guides pinpoint fixes for inertial parameters, joint limits, damping values, and collision hulls.

### 3.3 Scene-Level Assembly and CEM Placement Optimization
Once individual objects are generated, the overall scene is assembled.
- Step 4 (Deterministic Assembly): Objects are initially arranged by snapping the child's bottom face onto the parent's top surface according to the scene tree. While this eliminates floating artifacts, slight continuous misalignments cause interpenetration and scale discrepancies.
- Step 5 (CEM Refinement): For each object, a 4-DoF perturbation vector $z_i \in \mathbb{R}^4$ is defined, covering horizontal translation $(\Delta x, \Delta y)$, yaw rotation $\Delta \psi$, and isotropic log-scale $\log s$. Height is excluded to maintain surface contact. Using the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM), $N$ candidate layouts are sampled each iteration and evaluated under free drop in Isaac Sim.

A hybrid reward function drives optimization: SDF-based penetration penalty $D_{\mathrm{pen}}$, drift penalty during dropping $D_{\mathrm{drift}}$, and an MLLM-judged semantic score $S_{\mathrm{sem}}$ comparing relative positions and scales to the original image. Updating the Gaussian distribution using elite samples rapidly converges the layout toward a physically stable and visually faithful configuration.

captions.F3: Comparison of object-level URDF reconstruction results. Compared to existing methods (such as URDF-Anything+ and Articraft), NeoWorld-Pro (Ours) faithfully reproduces not only complex geometries like carts, baskets, and phone stands, but also their articulated kinematics (Ours Articulated).
captions.F4: Scene reconstruction comparison on the synthetic scene dataset. Across tabletop and room layouts where baseline methods (TabletopGen, VIGA, SAGE) miss or substitute objects, NeoWorld-Pro preserves object categories, relative scales, and orientations with high accuracy.

sections.heading: Superior Articulation Accuracy and Stable Simulation Performance
sections.summary: Evaluations on a new benchmark with 90 articulated categories and 30 scenes show that NeoWorld-Pro outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in single-object geometry and articulation accuracy, achieves a 0% scene interpenetration rate, and significantly improves downstream robotic task success (e.g., test-tube insertion).
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup and Benchmark
For comprehensive evaluation, the authors built a synthetic dataset of 30 USD scenes spanning 90 articulated object categories. The scenes feature severe occlusions and overlaps, each paired with downstream robotic manipulation tasks.

For single-object baselines, PhysX-Anything, URDF-Anything+, Articulate-Anything, and Articraft were evaluated. For scene reconstruction, TabletopGen, VIGA, and SAGE were compared.

### 4.2 Single-Object Reconstruction Performance
Evaluations covered appearance (SSIM, LPIPS, CLIP), geometry (Chamfer Distance, F-score, Uni3D similarity), and articulation fidelity.
- Appearance and Geometry: NeoWorld-Pro achieved top scores in LPIPS and CLIP similarity, as well as the highest F-score accuracy.
- Articulation: Generated joint actuation videos were compared against ground truth. NeoWorld-Pro dramatically reduced the articulation miss rate compared to baselines, while significantly cutting axis and pivot orientation errors.

### 4.3 Full Scene Assembly Performance
Scene-level metrics (Table 3) evaluated interpenetration rate (S-Pen), part self-collision rate (P-Pen), and stability under gravity (S-Stab, O-Stab) inside the physics engine.
- NeoWorld-Pro achieved a 0% scene interpenetration rate, whereas baseline methods suffered collision rates ranging from tens of percent up to 100%.
- It preserved over 90% scene stability under gravity, creating stable environments where objects do not spontaneously collapse.
- When tested on real-world photos, it demonstrated robustness against messy backgrounds and occlusions, faithfully recovering the articulated mechanics of key furniture and tools (Figure 5).

### 4.4 Downstream Robot Manipulation Validation
A fine-grained peg-in-hole task was conducted: picking a test tube and inserting it into a rack slot. Despite tight tolerances where millimeter-level layout errors cause failure, scenes reconstructed by NeoWorld-Pro allowed open-loop end-effector trajectories specified by the MLLM to execute successfully.

### 4.5 Ablation Study
Ablation experiments (Tables 4 and 5) revealed crucial design insights:
- Removing the semantic reward ($S_{\mathrm{sem}}$) yields physically stable layouts that deviate significantly from the visual scales and positions in the source image.
- Removing the simulator-in-the-loop critic leads to open-loop failures, causing severe initial intersections and tumble collapses upon dropping.
- Both penetration penalty ($D_{\mathrm{pen}}$) and drift penalty ($D_{\mathrm{drift}}$) in CEM correlate directly with downstream manipulation success; combining them is essential for high task completion rates.

captions.F5: Reconstruction results from single real-world images. Even from cluttered office desks and workbench photos with complex backgrounds, key objects are accurately segmented and functional articulations (e.g., opening glasses cases, pressing keyboard keys) are faithfully reproduced.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Work: Expanding to Deformables and Fluids
sections.summary: NeoWorld-Pro shows that combining program synthesis with physical simulation loops can generate high-quality, simulation-ready interactive environments from a single photo. Currently limited to quasi-static rigid and articulated bodies, scaling to continuous media like cloth and fluids, as well as dense scenes with over 10 objects, remains future work.
sections.details:
NeoWorld-Pro demonstrates the power of unifying procedural program synthesis and closed-loop simulation feedback (physics-in-the-loop) for building simulation-ready 3D spaces from single images. Overcoming the physical breakdowns common in direct mesh regression and retrieval methods, it marks a major milestone toward automated digital twin creation for robot learning.

Nonetheless, the paper highlights several limitations:
- It is restricted to quasi-static simulations of rigid and articulated objects with revolute or prismatic joints. Highly deformable materials (e.g., garments, cloth), fluids, and granular media (e.g., sand) cannot be easily formulated in URDFs and are currently out of scope.
- Evaluated scenes currently contain fewer than 10 objects. Scaling and validating the framework on ultra-dense, complex scenes with dozens or hundreds of items remains an open challenge.

sections.heading: Appendix: CEM Optimization Details and Diverse Robot Tasks
sections.summary: The appendix details technical practices stabilizing the CEM scene optimization—such as log-scale parameterization and adaptive standard deviation tuning—as well as the diverse manipulation tasks designed for the benchmark.
sections.details:
### CEM Placement Optimization Details (Appendix B)
Several key design choices ensure efficient and stable scene optimization:
- Bounding Box Scale Initialization: Because Blender procedurally generates objects in arbitrary modeling units, object dimensions are first aligned to the estimated 3D bounding boxes from Step 1.
- Log-Scale Space ($\log s$): Representing scale perturbations in log space prevents non-physical negative scales and ensures symmetric, smooth exploration of resizing.
- Adaptive Search Standard Deviation: The horizontal translation standard deviation $\sigma_{xy}$ is set to 5% of the object's 3D bounding box diagonal. This enables fine-grained adjustments for small objects and broader exploration for large furniture (with yaw rotation standard deviation $\sigma_\psi = 15^\circ$ and scale $\sigma_{\log s} = 0.1$).

### Benchmark Task Suite (Appendix A)
The dataset incorporates diverse robotic tasks that require both accurate articulation and precise spatial positioning, including opening a refrigerator to insert a beverage, cutting with scissors, typing on a keyboard, and unfolding a folding chair (Figure 6).

captions.F6: Examples of benchmark scenes and associated robot manipulation tasks. Defined tasks include drawer opening, bottle pumping, and chair unfolding, none of which can be completed in simulation unless both joint kinematics and spatial arrangements are accurate.

takeaways: Representing 3D assets as executable Blender Python scripts rather than direct meshes allows MLLM commonsense reasoning to logically extrapolate occluded interior structures.

Because generating a perfect 3D scene in an open-loop pass is brittle, running drop and collision tests in a physics engine and feeding failure logs/videos back to the MLLM for local code edits is remarkably effective.

Decoupling the refinement—assigning discrete kinematic structure and parameter tuning to MLLM code edits while delegating continuous spatial layouts (position, rotation, scale) to CEM optimization—yields a robust pipeline.
limitations: Confined to rigid and articulated bodies; it does not model complex deformable materials like cloth, paper, fluids, or granular substances.
Benchmark evaluations are limited to scenes with fewer than 10 objects; scalability to dense environments with hundreds of interacting items is unverified.
Iterative physics simulations in Isaac Sim and repeated MLLM inference calls during each validation cycle require noticeable computation time, making it unsuitable for real-time generation.
